answers.text: Until an HTTP layer exists, refund_order() is called from Python by staff-run code (a shell or a script run by an operator). There is no caller identity check yet; the plan's role check is open question 8. The HTTP route is open question 1.

refund_order() makes exactly one provider call per invocation and does not retry on its own. Retries happen only in reconcile_refunds(), which re-sends the same idempotency key for each pending refund, up to 3 attempts, then leaves it pending for staff.

Threshold is 15 minutes after the refund's created_at. If the provider lookup itself fails, the refund stays pending and is retried on the next reconcile run. If the provider says the refund is still in progress, it stays pending and is checked again on the next run.

The plan assumes the provider can be asked by idempotency key or provider refund id, and that it reports in-progress distinctly from not-found. Whether the real provider does this is open question 6. Until that is known, reconcile cannot tell "never received" from "still processing" with certainty, so the plan treats an unanswered lookup as pending, never as failed.

The lock is a file lock on a sidecar lock file next to orders.json, so it works across processes. A threading lock alone would not. Chosen because the app may run as several processes. Changed in step 2 to say so.

status is recomputed by one function every time an order is saved: refunded if the succeeded quantities equal the bought quantities for every item, partially_refunded if any succeeded refund exists, otherwise placed. It is recomputed on refund apply, including when reconcile moves a refund to succeeded. Pending and failed refunds do not change status.

All refunded items are restocked. Damaged or non-returnable goods are out of scope for this plan. Restock is written in the same save as the status update and the refund status change, so they succeed or fail together.

Current code has no tax, shipping or discount: total() is the sum of PRICES times quantities, and this plan keeps that. amount_cents is the sum of unit_prices times quantities at order time. Any future tax or discount would need its own fields and is not in scope.

The flag is an environment variable, REFUNDS_ENABLED, read at startup; an operator sets it. "Reconcile has run cleanly in staging" is not yet defined; I am leaving that as an open question rather than inventing a threshold.

answers.text: Each refund record gets `attempts` (int, starts at 0) and `last_attempt_at`. refund_order()'s provider call counts as attempt 1. Reconcile re-sends only while attempts is below 3. Changed in the data table.

The three cases are told apart by the lookup, not by the status field. For every pending refund, reconcile first asks the provider by idempotency key. If the provider has it, reconcile applies that result. If not, it re-sends with the same key, which is safe because the key stops a duplicate. A crash before the call and a save failure after success both end in the same path: the lookup or re-send resolves them. The "unknown" wording in step 5 is dropped; every pending refund goes through the same path.

Exact order for each pending refund in reconcile: (1) lookup by key. (2) If found and succeeded, apply succeeded. If found and in progress, leave pending. (3) If not found and attempts < 3, re-send with the same key and increment attempts. (4) If not found and attempts = 3, leave pending and flag it for staff. A refund becomes `failed` only when the provider definitively declines a send. "Not found" is never enough to mark failed, because a delayed request could still complete later and cause a second refund. Changed the table row to match.

The apply step re-reads orders.json under the file lock, finds the refund by id, and changes it only if it is still `pending`. The STOCK increment and status recompute happen in that same save, and only on the pending-to-succeeded transition. Reconcile uses the same apply function, so a refund that both paths touch is changed once; the second writer sees it is no longer pending and does nothing.

items is a dict {name: qty}, the same shape place_order() uses. Validation and the append of the pending record happen inside one lock hold, so two calls cannot both pass the check. The provider call happens after the lock is released.

refund_order() returns a dict in the same style as place_order(), and never raises for expected cases: {"status": "succeeded", "refund": ...}, {"status": "pending", "refund": ...} (for provider unknowns, and for the save-failed-after-success case, because the pending record was saved first and reconcile resolves it), {"status": "failed", "reason": ...} (provider declined), and {"status": "rejected", "reason": ...} (validation errors, flag off, or a pending refund already covers those items). An unexpected exception is logged and the record stays pending.

With REFUNDS_ENABLED off, refund_order() returns {"status": "rejected", "reason": "refunds disabled"} and creates no record. reconcile_refunds() does not check the flag and always runs, so refunds already in flight are never stranded when the flag is turned off.

Migration is a one-off operator script, `python -m src.migrate_orders`, run once before the flag is enabled. It adds status "placed", refunds [], and backfilled amount_cents and unit_prices, and sets migrated: true. Refund logic does not treat migrated orders differently; the flag is kept only as an audit marker.

Yes. A re-send that is declined becomes `failed` with `error` set. A re-send with an unknown result stays `pending`, sets `error`, and counts toward the 3 attempts. Changed in step 5.

With items=None, the refund covers the remaining quantity per item: bought minus succeeded minus pending. If nothing remains, the result is `rejected` with reason "nothing left to refund". Changed in step 4.

answers.text: Yes. Whenever the provider confirms a refund as completed, reconcile applies `succeeded`, even if `needs_attention` is set. A refund reaching `succeeded` or `failed` clears `needs_attention`. Nothing else clears it. Changed in step 5.

Yes, a re-send could race an in-flight request if the process died. Reconcile never acts on a refund younger than 15 minutes, and its first step is always a lookup by key. If the provider reports the original as in progress, reconcile does not re-send. The idempotency key covers the rest: a re-send with the same key returns the original outcome, not a second refund. Whether the provider does this is open question 6. Changed in step 5.

Failed records are kept forever as audit history. The error text says why, for example "charge already refunded". The fix is for staff to check the charge at the provider. A new refund request creates a new record and does not reuse the failed one. Changed in the provider table.

The lock is an OS-level file lock (msvcrt on Windows, fcntl elsewhere), not a lock-file-exists check, so a crashed process releases it and no stale lock forms. A caller waits up to 10 seconds. If it still cannot get the lock, the call returns `rejected` with reason "store busy" for a new request, and for an apply step the refund stays `pending` and reconcile picks it up. Changed in step 2.
Yes. The `amount_cents` computed from `unit_prices` is the value passed to `charge()`, and the `payment` field is the id `charge()` returns. The total is the same `total(items)` figure in `app.py`.

The refund id is a UUID4 generated when the pending record is created. It doubles as the idempotency key. Whether the provider keeps keys long enough for reconcile is part of open question 6; this plan requires keys to be kept at least as long as the reconcile window plus a week. Changed in the refund record table.

answers.text: The first call saves the pending record with attempts: 1 and last_attempt_at set to now, both in the same save and before the provider call. A declined or unknown result changes only status (for declined), error, and updated_at. Neither attempts nor last_attempt_at changes when the result is applied. Changed in step 4.
The wait is measured from the later of created_at and last_attempt_at, so a re-send is not attempted again until 15 minutes after the previous send. Changed in step 5.

The lookup has five outcomes: completed, in_progress, not_found, failed, and unknown (the lookup call itself errored). "failed" means the provider has the refund and says it did not move money, so reconcile applies `failed` with the provider's reason. Changed in step 5.

Deploy order: (1) deploy the new code to all instances, with REFUNDS_ENABLED off. (2) Run `python -m src.migrate_orders`. The migration is idempotent: it skips any order that already has `amount_cents`, so orders placed by the new code in between are not touched. Old-code instances must be stopped before step 1 completes, because they would write orders without the new fields. Changed in step 8.
The `refund` value is the full refund record exactly as stored, with every field listed in the refund record table. Changed in step 4.

payments.py becomes a `Provider` class with three methods: `charge(card_token, amount_cents)`, `refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key)`, and `lookup_refund(idempotency_key)`. The last returns `{"state": completed|in_progress|not_found|failed|unknown, "provider_refund_id": ...}`. The real implementation is in payments.py. The fake lives in tests/ and is injected into app.py through a module-level PROVIDER variable. Changed in step 3.

teachbacks.text:
This is a draft plan, so nothing below exists yet. I'm describing the intended design. I follow one request: staff refund part of a placed order, and the provider times out.

1. **Prerequisite: the order must hold money facts.** Today an order has only `id`, `customer`, `items`, `payment`. Step 1 of the plan changes `place_order()` to also store `amount_cents`, `unit_prices` (a price snapshot), `status: "placed"` and `refunds: []`. Orders are saved in `data/orders.json`, which holds the state. Old orders are backfilled once by `python -m src.migrate_orders`, which uses the current `PRICES` table and sets `migrated: true`. The migration runs after the new code is deployed everywhere and before `REFUNDS_ENABLED` is turned on. It skips orders that already have `amount_cents`.

2. **Trigger.** An operator calls `refund_order(order_id, items=None, reason="")` from Python. There is no HTTP route yet and no caller identity check. `items` is `{name: qty}`. `None` means "everything remaining", which is bought minus succeeded minus pending. The flag `REFUNDS_ENABLED` is an environment variable, read at startup, and it defaults to off.

3. **Take the lock and validate.** All reads and writes of `orders.json` go through one helper. It uses an OS-level file lock on a sidecar file and waits up to 10 seconds. If it can't get the lock, a new request returns `rejected` with "store busy". While holding the lock, the code does these things:
   - It loads the order.
   - It checks that the order exists, the flag is on, and each requested quantity is at most bought minus succeeded minus pending.
   - It computes `amount_cents` from `unit_prices`.
   - It appends a refund record with a new UUID4 `id`, `status: pending`, `attempts: 1` and `last_attempt_at` set to now.
   - It saves to a temp file and uses `os.replace`.

   The check and the append happen under the same lock hold, so two simultaneous calls can't both pass. Validation failures, a flag that is off, and overlap with a pending refund all return `{"status":"rejected","reason":...}` and create no record. Overlap gives "refund in progress", and an empty remainder gives "nothing left to refund".

4. **Release the lock and call the provider.** The code makes exactly one `PROVIDER.refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key=refund id)` call, with no retry. The provider is a `Provider` class in `payments.py`, and tests inject a fake through the module variable `PROVIDER`. `refund()` catches provider exceptions and returns one of `succeeded` (with a provider refund id), `declined`, or `unknown`.

5. **Re-take the lock and apply the result.** The code re-reads `orders.json` and finds the refund by id. It applies the result only if the refund is still `pending`; otherwise it does nothing. In one save it:
   - sets the refund status
   - adds the refunded quantities back to the in-memory `STOCK`, but only on the `pending` to `succeeded` transition
   - recomputes the order `status` (`refunded` if every item is fully succeeded, `partially_refunded` if any refund succeeded, otherwise `placed`)

   The caller gets one of these results:
   - `succeeded`, with the full refund record
   - `failed`, with the reason, when the provider declined. The record becomes `failed` with `error`, stock and order status don't change, and a later refund for the same items is allowed.
   - `pending`, with the refund record, on timeout, connection reset, 5xx, an unmapped exception, or a save failure after provider success. The record stays `pending` and stock is unchanged.

6. **Our example: timeout.** The refund stays `pending` on disk and the caller sees `pending`. While it is pending, any overlapping refund request is rejected, which prevents double refunds. The refund id is the idempotency key, so a re-send can't create a second refund.

7. **Reconciliation.** `reconcile_refunds()` is run by an operator with `python -m src.reconcile_refunds`. It scans all orders. It ignores `REFUNDS_ENABLED`, so refunds in flight are never stranded. It handles only pending refunds that are at least 15 minutes past the later of `created_at` and `last_attempt_at`. For each one it calls `lookup_refund(key)` without holding the lock, then branches on the state:
   - `completed`: apply `succeeded`. This restocks, updates order status, and clears `needs_attention`.
   - `failed`: apply `failed` with the provider's reason.
   - `in_progress` or `unknown`: leave it pending and check again next run.
   - `not_found` with attempts below 3: under the lock, increment `attempts` and set `last_attempt_at`, then save and release. Re-send with the same key, then re-take the lock and apply the result. A decline becomes `failed`. An unknown result stays `pending`, sets `error`, and still counts as an attempt.
   - `not_found` with attempts at 3: leave it pending, set `needs_attention: true`, and write an ERROR log line. A human decides.

   A refund becomes `failed` only on a definitive decline, never just because the lookup says "not found". The script prints counts (checked, succeeded, failed, still pending, needs_attention) plus the order and refund ids that need attention.

8. **Crash cases.** If the process crashes after the pending save, the refund stays `pending` on disk, the caller gets nothing back, and reconcile looks it up and re-sends if needed. If the provider succeeded but our save failed, reconcile finds the completed refund and marks it `succeeded`.

9. **Rollout.** Ship steps 1–2 first (the stored fields and the lock). Then deploy new code to all instances with the flag off and stop any old-code instance. Then run the migration. Enable `REFUNDS_ENABLED` only after reconcile has run in staging. Tests use a fake provider and cover partial refunds, over-refunds, duplicate requests, and reconcile finding a completed refund, including one confirmed after `needs_attention` was set.
gaps: Which real payment provider is used, and whether it supports idempotency keys and lookup by key (open question 6). Without this, reconcile can't work and the plan has no safe automatic path.
How long the provider keeps idempotency keys. The document says it must be at least the 'reconcile window plus a week', but never defines the reconcile window.
How staff reach this: no HTTP layer exists (open question 1). The README mentions POST /orders and emailed receipts, but neither exists. No role check or caller identity is defined (open question 8).
What the HTTP route would return or accept, or what 'restrict to staff' means in practice.
How reconcile gets scheduled, and what happens if two reconcile runs, or reconcile and a live refund_order, overlap on the same refund beyond the apply-only-if-still-pending rule.
How the lock behaves in reconcile apply steps when the 10-second wait is exceeded, beyond 'stays pending'. It's also unclear what a caller sees if the lock fails at the apply step in refund_order.
How stock is persisted. STOCK is in memory and resets on restart, so restocking is lost (open question 3). Overselling in place_order is also unsolved (open question 4).
Who sees needs_attention and how (open question 10), and what the human actually does to resolve it.
What 'reconcile ran cleanly in staging' means (open question 9).
Whether refunds have a time limit (open question 7), whether arbitrary-amount refunds are needed (open question 5), and whether refunds send an email notice (open question 2).

How the provider is told which payment to refund: the order's payment field is called the 'provider charge id', but the document doesn't show its exact shape. The charge() signature also changes from the current stub to take card_token and amount_cents, and how place_order obtains the card token isn't stated.

What happens to a declined re-send in reconcile for the order and stock, which the document only says becomes failed. It also doesn't say how an unmapped exception is alerted ('log, alert') or where the alert goes.
The exact format of the timestamps, and the log format and destination for ERROR lines.
teachbacks.notes:
Teach-back round 1 could not explain or got wrong:
- The "reconcile window" in the idempotency-key requirement was undefined. Fixed: now "at least one week", with the 15-minute wait named.
- Caller result when the lock fails at the apply step was missing. Fixed: returns {"status": "pending"}; reconcile applies later.
- Two overlapping reconcile runs, or reconcile plus a live refund_order, were not addressed. Fixed: a new paragraph in step 5.
- Timestamp format was missing. Fixed: ISO 8601 UTC.
- The ERROR log destination was missing. Fixed: standard logging, logger shopfront.refunds.
- charge() and card_token were unclear. Fixed: same signature; token handling out of scope.
- The "refund in progress" and "store busy" reasons were not named. Fixed in step 4.
Still open (already in the open questions): the real provider and key lookup (6), the HTTP layer and staff identity (1, 8), the alert channel (10), staging bar (9), stock persistence (3), overselling (4), receipts (2), refund window (7), and arbitrary amounts (5).

teachbacks.text:
This is a plan (a draft, no code written yet) for letting staff refund placed orders. I'll follow one request: staff refund part of order 7, and the provider times out. I'll mention the other outcomes where the document covers them.

**0. Preconditions (set up before any refund can run)**
1. Orders live in `data/orders.json`. The new `place_order()` (plan step 1) stores `amount_cents`, `unit_prices` (a price snapshot), `status: "placed"` and `refunds: []` on each order, alongside the existing `id`, `customer`, `items` and `payment`. The `payment` field is the provider's charge id, which refunds reference.
2. Old orders are backfilled once by `python -m src.migrate_orders`. It is idempotent and skips orders that already have `amount_cents`. It runs after the new code is deployed everywhere and before `REFUNDS_ENABLED` is turned on.
3. `REFUNDS_ENABLED` is an environment variable. It is read at startup, set by an operator, and defaults to off.
4. All reads and writes of `orders.json` go through one helper. It takes a cross-process OS file lock on a sidecar lock file and waits up to 10 seconds. It writes to a temp file and then `os.replace`s it into place.

**1. The trigger**
1. A staff member, working as an operator in a Python shell or script, calls `refund_order(order_id, items=None, reason="")` in `app.py`. For example, `refund_order(7, {"mug": 1}, "damaged")`.
2. There is no HTTP route yet and no identity check. The route `POST /orders/<id>/refunds` is only planned, if an HTTP layer ever exists.
3. `items=None` means "refund everything remaining". Remaining is bought minus succeeded minus pending.

**2. Validate and record intent (first lock hold)**
1. The function takes the file lock and loads the order.
2. It validates three things:
   - The order exists.
   - The flag is on.
   - Each requested quantity is at most bought minus (succeeded + pending).
3. If validation fails, it returns `{"status": "rejected", "reason": ...}` and creates no record. The reasons are:
   - "refunds disabled"
   - "nothing left to refund"
   - "refund in progress" (an overlapping pending refund)
   - "store busy" (the lock wait timed out)
4. If validation passes, it computes `amount_cents` from the order's `unit_prices`.
5. It appends a refund record with these fields:
   - `id`: a new UUID4, which doubles as the provider idempotency key.
   - `status`: `pending`.
   - `attempts`: 1.
   - `last_attempt_at`: now (ISO 8601 UTC).
   - `created_at` and `updated_at`.
   - `items`, `amount_cents` and `reason`.
6. It saves this pending record before calling the provider. The check and the append happen in the same lock hold, so two simultaneous calls cannot both pass.
7. It then releases the lock.

**3. The provider call (no lock held)**
1. `Provider.refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key)` is called once. `refund_order()` never retries.
2. The method catches provider exceptions and returns one of three results:
   - `succeeded` (with the provider refund id)
   - `declined`
   - `unknown` (timeout, network error, 5xx)

**4. Apply the result (second lock hold)**
1. The function re-takes the lock with the same 10-second wait. It re-reads `orders.json` and finds the refund by id.
2. It applies the result only if the refund is still `pending`. Otherwise it applies nothing. Reconcile uses the same apply function.
3. The outcomes are:
   - **Succeeded:** the refund becomes `succeeded` and `provider_refund_id` is set. `STOCK` is incremented by the refunded quantities. The order `status` is recomputed (`refunded` if every item's succeeded quantity equals the bought quantity, `partially_refunded` if any refund succeeded, otherwise `placed`). All of this happens in one save. The caller gets `{"status": "succeeded", "refund": <record>}`.
   - **Declined:** the refund becomes `failed` with `error` set. Stock and order status are unchanged. The caller gets `{"status": "failed", "reason": ...}`. Staff check the charge at the provider and may start a new refund. The failed record stays as history and does not block later refunds.
   - **Unknown (our running example):** the refund stays `pending` and `error` is recorded. Stock and order status are unchanged. The caller gets `{"status": "pending", "refund": ...}`.
4. If the lock can't be taken, or the save fails after the provider succeeded, the refund stays `pending` on disk and the caller gets `pending`.
5. If an unexpected exception occurs, it is logged and the record stays `pending`.
6. If the process crashes after the pending save, the record stays `pending` on disk and nothing is returned to the caller.
7. While a refund is pending, any overlapping request is rejected with "refund in progress". This is the guard against double refunds.

**5. Reconciliation (resolves pending refunds)**
1. An operator runs `python -m src.reconcile_refunds` from the project root. A schedule may come later. It scans all orders.
2. It does not check `REFUNDS_ENABLED`, so in-flight refunds are not stranded.
3. It handles only `pending` refunds that are at least 15 minutes past the later of `created_at` and `last_attempt_at`.
4. For each such refund it calls `lookup_refund(idempotency_key)` without holding the lock. The result decides what happens next:
   - `completed`: apply `succeeded`, which restocks and updates the order status.
   - `failed`: the provider says no money moved. Apply `failed` with the provider's reason.
   - `in_progress` or `unknown`: leave it `pending` and check again on the next run.
   - `not_found` with `attempts` below 3:
     1. Under the lock, increment `attempts`, set `last_attempt_at` and save.
     2. Release the lock.
     3. Re-send with the same key.
     4. Re-take the lock and apply the result. A decline becomes `failed`. An unknown stays `pending`, sets `error`, and still counts toward the 3 attempts.
   - `not_found` with `attempts` at 3: leave it `pending`, set `needs_attention: true`, and write an ERROR line to the `shopfront.refunds` logger. A human decides what to do. The flag is cleared if the refund later reaches `succeeded` or `failed`.
5. The command prints counts (checked, succeeded, failed, still pending, needs_attention) plus the ids that need attention.
6. Overlapping runs are safe in the cases the document covers:
   - Reconcile runs, or a reconcile run and a live call, share the same idempotency key, so the provider makes at most one refund.
   - Apply only changes a refund that is still `pending`, so the result is written once.
   - `attempts` may be double-incremented. This is harmless, because it only brings `needs_attention` sooner.
7. A refund becomes `failed` only on a definitive decline or a provider `failed` lookup. "Not found" alone never fails it, because a delayed request could still complete and cause a second refund.

**6. Rollout**
1. Ship plan steps 1–2 first (stored fields and safe writes).
2. Deploy the new code to all instances with the flag off, and stop any old-code instance.
3. Run the migration.
4. Enable `REFUNDS_ENABLED` only after reconcile has run in staging.
5. Tests use a fake provider that lives in `tests/` and is injected through the module-level `PROVIDER` variable.

teachbacks.text:
This is a draft plan, so nothing runs yet. I'll walk through one refund of a placed order, from the staff call to the end, including the failure paths. Names come from the document.

**Setup before any refund can happen**

1. Placing an order (`place_order()` in `src/app.py`) will change. It checks stock, charges, decrements stock, then appends to `data/orders.json`. The new version also stores `amount_cents`, a `unit_prices` snapshot, `status: "placed"` and `refunds: []`. The order's `payment` field is the provider's charge id, and refunds reference it. The order file holds all of this state.
2. Old orders get the same fields from `python -m src.migrate_orders`. An operator runs it once, after the new code is deployed and before `REFUNDS_ENABLED` is turned on. It skips orders that already have `amount_cents`.
3. All reads and writes of `orders.json` go through one helper. It takes an OS-level file lock on a sidecar file and waits up to 10 seconds. It writes to a temp file and then `os.replace`s it into place.

**Following one refund, e.g. staff refund 1 of 2 items on order 7**

4. **Trigger.** There is no HTTP layer yet. An operator calls `refund_order(order_id, items=None, reason="")` from Python. `items` is `{name: qty}`. `None` means "everything remaining", which is bought minus succeeded minus pending.
5. **Validate and record, under one lock hold.**
   - The code loads the order and checks that the order exists and the flag is on.
   - It checks each requested quantity against bought minus succeeded minus pending.
   - It computes `amount_cents` from the order's `unit_prices`.
   - It appends a refund record with `status: pending`, a new UUID4 `id`, `attempts: 1`, `last_attempt_at` set to now, and `created_at`/`updated_at`.
   - It saves the record before any provider call.
   - The check and the append happen in the same lock hold, so two simultaneous calls can't both pass.
   - If validation fails, the caller gets `rejected` and no record is created. The reasons are "refunds disabled", "nothing left to refund", "refund in progress" (overlap with a pending refund) and "store busy" (the lock wait timed out). The document does not name the reason returned for an unknown order or an over-quantity request.
6. **Provider call, with no lock held.** The code calls `PROVIDER.refund(payment_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key)`. The refund `id` is the idempotency key. There is exactly one call and no retry here. `Provider.refund` returns one of three results: `succeeded` (with a provider refund id), `declined`, or `unknown` (timeout, network error, 5xx). It catches provider exceptions itself.
7. **Apply the result.** The code takes the lock again (up to 10 seconds), re-reads `orders.json`, and finds the refund by id. It applies the result only if the refund is still `pending`.
   - On `succeeded`: the refund becomes `succeeded` and stores `provider_refund_id`. Stock is incremented by the refunded quantities. Order `status` is recomputed (`refunded` if every item is fully refunded, otherwise `partially_refunded` if any refund succeeded, otherwise `placed`). All of this happens in one save. The caller gets `{"status": "succeeded", "refund": ...}`.
   - On `declined`: the refund becomes `failed` with `error`. Stock and order status are unchanged. The caller gets `{"status": "failed", "reason": ...}`. Staff check the charge at the provider and may start a new refund. A failed refund doesn't block a later one for the same items.
   - On `unknown`: the refund stays `pending` and the caller gets `{"status": "pending", "refund": ...}`.
   - If the lock can't be retaken, or the save fails after a provider success, the refund stays `pending` on disk and the caller gets `pending`. Reconcile resolves it later.
   - An unexpected exception is logged and the record stays `pending`.
   - If the refund is no longer pending (something else resolved it), nothing is applied.

**Reconciliation, which handles anything left pending**

8. **Trigger.** An operator runs `python -m src.reconcile_refunds`. There is no schedule yet. It scans all orders and picks pending refunds that are at least 15 minutes past the later of `created_at` and `last_attempt_at`. It ignores `REFUNDS_ENABLED`.
9. **Lookup.** For each refund it calls `lookup_refund(idempotency_key)` without holding the lock. What it does next depends on the state returned:
   - `completed`: apply `succeeded`, with restock and status recompute, using the same apply function as step 7.
   - `failed`: apply `failed` with the provider's reason.
   - `in_progress` or `unknown`: leave it pending until the next run.
   - `not_found` with attempts below 3: under the lock, increment `attempts`, set `last_attempt_at` and save. Then release the lock and re-send with the same key. Then retake the lock and apply the result. A decline becomes `failed`. An unknown stays `pending`, sets `error`, and still counts as an attempt.
   - `not_found` with attempts at 3: leave it pending, set `needs_attention: true`, and write an ERROR line to logger `shopfront.refunds`.
10. **Safety against double refunds.** The same key is used every time, so the provider makes at most one refund. The apply step only changes a refund that is still `pending`. Two overlapping runs may double-increment `attempts`, which the plan calls harmless. "Not found" never makes a refund `failed`, because a delayed request could still complete.
11. **Output and manual resolution.** The script prints counts (checked, succeeded, failed, still pending, needs_attention) and the order and refund ids that need attention. A `needs_attention` refund is resolved by hand. The operator checks the provider dashboard for the key. They then either wait for the next run or, if the provider confirms nothing happened, start a new refund. `needs_attention` is cleared when the refund reaches `succeeded` or `failed`.

**Rollout**

12. Steps 1–2 ship first. Then all instances get the new code with `REFUNDS_ENABLED` off, and old-code instances are stopped. Then the migration runs. The flag is enabled only after reconcile has run in staging. The flag is read at startup and defaults to off. Step 6 (an HTTP route, `POST /orders/<id>/refunds`, restricted to staff) comes only if an HTTP layer exists. Step 7 lists tests using a fake provider injected through the module-level `PROVIDER` variable.
gaps: Whether an HTTP layer exists. The route in step 6 depends on it, and the README and the code disagree (open question 1).

Which real payment provider is used, and whether it supports idempotency keys and lookup by key. Reconcile depends on this (open question 6). The document does not say how the real `charge`/`refund`/`lookup_refund` calls are made.
How `card_token` is obtained for `charge()`. The document says this is out of scope.
Who may call a refund and how that is checked. No caller identity check exists yet (open question 8).
The rejection reason for an unknown order id or a requested quantity above what is refundable. The listed reasons don't cover them.
How reconcile is scheduled. It runs on demand only.
Where `needs_attention` is surfaced beyond an ERROR log line (open question 10). There is also no tooling to force a status.
The bar for 'reconcile ran cleanly in staging' (open question 9).
`STOCK` is in memory and resets on restart, so restocking is lost. How or whether to persist it is undecided (open question 3).
Overselling in `place_order()` is not fixed by the file lock (open question 4).
Whether a refund limit window exists (open question 7). Whether arbitrary-amount refunds are needed (open question 5). Whether a refund sends an email notice (open question 2).

What the caller sees if the first lock wait for the pending-record save times out is covered ('store busy'). What happens when a lock timeout occurs during a reconcile apply is only partly covered: the refund stays pending. How the process behaves if the crash happens between provider success and the first save is not covered beyond 'reconcile looks up'.
How the pending-refund overlap check treats the `items=None` case when the quantity remaining is partial. This is not detailed beyond 'bought minus succeeded minus pending'.

The document says the first send counts as attempt 1, but it doesn't say whether the 15-minute wait applies to a refund whose live call returned `unknown`. It does follow from the rule on `last_attempt_at`, so this is inferred.

holes: Q4: For a pending refund that already got a provider result of 'unknown', how does reconcile tell 'provider never received it' from 'provider is still processing it'? Does the provider API expose that? (author: The plan assumes the provider can be asked by idempotency key or provider refund id, and that it reports in-progress distinctly from not-found. Whether the real provider does this is open question 6. Until that is known, reconcile cannot tell "never received" from "still processing" with certainty, so the plan treats an unanswered lookup as pending, never as failed.)
